one_liner: Multi-architecture ROP gadget finder in Rust; much faster than the Python tool Ropper on large binaries.
what_it_does: A command-line tool that scans an object file (PE/COFF, ELF or Mach-O) or a raw blob for ROP gadgets in its executable regions, de-duplicates them, and prints each unique gadget's mnemonic with every address it appears at. It is standalone tooling, not a library drop-in: the interface is a CLI with flags for architecture, endianness, gadget length bounds (--min-insns, --max-insns, default 2-10), which terminating instructions to allow (ret by default, optional call/jmp) and a regex pre-filter. It covers arm, arm64, x86, x86_64, mips, mips64, ppc, ppc64, riscv, riscv64, sparc64 and s390x.
how_it_is_fast: The gadget search is embarrassingly parallel over a precomputed list of valid instruction start addresses (every byte on x86, every 4 bytes on fixed-width ISAs, every 2 bytes on RISC-V/s390x), fanned out with rayon; each worker thread holds its own Capstone handle in thread-local storage. A two-pass design does the bulk work without ever materialising mnemonic strings: the first pass stores only raw instruction bytes, de-duplicates them into a reversed-instruction tree (a trie rooted at each terminating instruction), and only the unique survivors are disassembled a second time to produce text, which the README says cuts both time and memory versus storing strings up front. The 100x+ gap over Ropper is mostly Rust and multithreading against a single-threaded Python tool.
when_to_use: Enumerating gadgets in very large binaries (browser engines, OS kernels, shared libraries tens to hundreds of MB) where a Python finder takes tens of minutes to hours.
Cross-architecture work: one tool for arm64, x86_64, mips, ppc, riscv, sparc64 and s390x, with architecture and endianness auto-detected from the object headers.
Pipelines that want de-duplicated output with all load addresses per gadget, pre-filtered by a Rust regex before writing.
Workflows that would otherwise dump all gadgets to a file and grep it (the author's own recommendation), on machines with many cores to feed rayon.
when_not_to_use: When you need gadget semantics, chain building, or a constraint/JOP solver: this only finds and prints gadgets (ret-terminated by default; call/jmp are opt-in flags), with no chaining or search over gadget effects.

When you need a validated speed figure: the published numbers are single untimed-hardware runs and the Ropper baseline is an estimate ('about 35 minutes', 'gave up after about 3 hours'), so treat the ratios as order-of-magnitude only.
Very small binaries where either tool finishes in well under a second and the parallel setup buys nothing.
If you need resilience to malformed input: the binary parse and segment/section reads use unwrap()/expect() throughout, so a file object cannot parse aborts the run with a panic rather than an error.

integration.dependencies: capstone 0.12 and capstone-sys 0.16 (link the Capstone engine), object 0.35 for file parsing, rayon 1.10, regex 1.10, clap 4.5, indicatif 0.17, itertools 0.12
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; a C toolchain to build the bundled Capstone via capstone-sys
integration.platforms: Host tool for any platform Rust+Capstone build on; the target binary may be any of the 12 supported ISAs regardless of host
integration.thread_safety: Single-process CLI; internally multithreaded with rayon, one Capstone handle per thread in TLS
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — a faster alternative to Ropper's gadget-finding, but a different CLI and output format, and it omits Ropper's chain-building and semantic features

gotchas: `cargo install inspector-gadget` builds capstone-sys from source, so a C compiler and the usual native-build setup are needed; the only published crate version is 0.3.0.
Output is a gadget mnemonic plus its list of addresses, not a ready chain; de-duplication means a gadget appears once with many addresses rather than once per address.

Terminating-instruction detection is hand-written per architecture (RISC-V and s390x match raw ret opcodes, s390x reg-operand counting drops to the capstone-sys C API); on RISC/CISC targets without clean Capstone call/jmp group tags the README warns the call/jmp options are 'less effective or non-functional'.
Relies on Capstone for all decoding, so it inherits Capstone's decode coverage and any decode bugs for a given ISA version (Capstone and Ropper versions behind the numbers are not stated).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: This is the only ROP gadget finder in the category; the disassembler siblings (iced, Zydis, Fadec, bddisasm, yaxpeax-x86, diStorm3) are decode-throughput libraries, not gadget search tools. Reach for inspector-gadget when the task is finding gadgets across many architectures fast; reach for one of those decoders when you are building your own analysis on raw instruction streams.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's unspecified 'test box' (no CPU, Capstone or Ropper version given), a single `time` run found all gadgets in an Android arm64 libmonochrome.so in 9.758 s versus Ropper's estimated ~35 min (about 215x), and in a Windows x86_64 xul.dll in 1m25.907s while Ropper was abandoned after ~3 hours (lower bound >125x). Both ratios are derived from page data; the Ropper side has no measured time and, per the README, Ropper did not de-duplicate or sort, so inspector-gadget does strictly more work, which strengthens the comparison rather than inflating it.
